summary: Specifies a negotiation mechanism for GSS-API so peers can choose a common security mechanism. If the chosen mechanism supports per-message integrity, the negotiation itself is protected against an attacker. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Two people who speak several languages first agree which one to use. This memo lets two programs agree on the secure method to use, and notice if a trickster interferes.

questions: what is the gss-api negotiation mechanism
subtitle: How two programs using GSS-API agree on a shared security mechanism, and notice if an attacker tampers with the choice.

tldr.problem: GSS-API lets peers set up a security context if they hold credentials for the same security mechanism, but it does not say how they find out which mechanism they have in common.
tldr.mechanism: SPNEGO is a pseudo mechanism: the initiator sends an ordered list of mechanisms, the acceptor picks one, and the real mechanism's tokens then travel inside SPNEGO tokens. If the chosen mechanism offers per-message integrity, MIC tokens over the mechanism list confirm nobody altered it.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2478 to fix defects and to interoperate with commonly deployed implementations, at the price of not interoperating with a strict RFC 2478 implementation.

today: RFC 4178 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2478, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Negotiation Problem
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743) is a generic interface that can sit on top of different security mechanisms. If two peers acquire credentials for the same mechanism, they can set up a security context. GSS-API itself does not say how the peers learn whether they share a mechanism.

SPNEGO (Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation) fills that gap. It is a pseudo security mechanism: it works in-band to find a common mechanism, then invokes the normal context establishment for the one selected. Callers of GSS-API only need to know about the new pseudo mechanism, not the negotiation tokens. A failure in the negotiation phase returns the major status code GSS_S_BAD_MECH.

Options inside the chosen mechanism are negotiated by that mechanism and are opaque to SPNEGO, so they are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Before two programs can talk securely, they must agree on how. SPNEGO is the little chat where they pick the method, so the programs using it do not have to think about it.

sections.title: The Negotiation Exchange
sections.content:
The model is simple. The initiator proposes a list of mechanisms in decreasing preference order, favorite first. The acceptor (also called the target) either takes the initiator's first choice or picks another from the list. If none is acceptable it rejects. The list must not contain SPNEGO itself or any mechanism for which the client has no credentials.

Unless the application sets a preference order, how the acceptor chooses is a local matter. Absent any policy, it SHALL choose the first mechanism in the initiator's list for which it has valid credentials.

To save a round trip, the initiator SHOULD put the first context token of its preferred mechanism into the first message. This is the optimistic mechanism token. It may be left out when the preferred mechanism is unlikely to be selected and the token is costly to generate.

The acceptor's first reply carries one of four states. After that, the selected mechanism's own tokens are wrapped in negotiation messages until both sides report GSS_S_COMPLETE. SPNEGO must also keep prot_ready_state false on return from GSS_Init_sec_context() and GSS_Accept_sec_context(), so a half-built context is not used for per-message calls that could clash with the MIC tokens.
sections.eli5: One child lists the games they like, favorite first. The other child picks the first one they also know how to play. If they share none, they stop.

sections.title: The Negotiation Tokens
sections.content:
SPNEGO messages are ASN.1 structures and MUST be encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). The pseudo mechanism is identified by the object identifier 1.3.6.1.5.5.2. Only the initial token uses the generic GSS-API token framing from RFC 2743; later tokens MUST NOT.

A NegotiationToken is a choice of two shapes. negTokenInit is the very first message, and only that message. Its mechTypes field lists the initiator's mechanisms in preference order. It may carry mechToken (the optimistic token) and mechListMIC. It also has a legacy reqFlags field, inherited from RFC 2478 and not integrity protected: initiators SHOULD omit it and acceptors MUST ignore it.

negTokenResp is used for every later message. Its negState field is REQUIRED in the first reply from the target and OPTIONAL after that. supportedMech appears only in the first reply and MUST be one of the offered mechanisms. responseToken carries the selected mechanism's own tokens, and mechListMIC may carry the integrity check.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of notes. The first note is the list of choices. Every note after that is an answer that says how things are going.

sections.title: Protecting the Mechanism List
sections.content:
Negotiation happens before any security exists, so an attacker could tamper with the list to force a weaker mechanism. SPNEGO closes this by having the peers check the list once the chosen mechanism's context is established. The check is a mechListMIC, a message integrity code made by calling GSS_GetMIC() with qop_req of 0 over the DER encoding of the MechTypeList value. It is not computed over the [0] MechTypeList wrapper.

If the selected mechanism has no integrity protection, no MIC token is used. If the accepted mechanism is the most preferred one of both initiator and acceptor, the MIC exchange is OPTIONAL. In every other case MIC tokens MUST be exchanged after the mechanism context is fully established. An acceptor signals that the exchange is required with the request-mic state in its first reply.

The detailed rules depend on who sends the last mechanism token. A missing required MIC, or a wrong one, terminates the negotiation with GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN. When a MIC is present and verifies, the receiver completes and answers with its own MIC and an accept-completed state, and the other side MUST verify it.
sections.eli5: After the two kids pick a game, they each show the list they remember writing. If the lists differ, someone has been messing with the paper, so they stop.

sections.title: Extending the Protocol
sections.content:
There are two extension routes. First, the ASN.1 structures MAY be expanded by IETF standards action, and implementations receiving unknown fields MUST ignore them.

Second, an initiator may include object identifiers that do not name a mechanism but a desired mechanism attribute, a variant. The acceptor can honor the request by preferring mechanisms with those attributes. The RFC expects the Kitten working group to standardize common attributes.

This interacts with the MIC rules. If the acceptor supports negotiating attributes that the initiator's preferred mechanism lacks, it MUST demand the MIC exchange, whether or not the initiator asked for those attributes.
sections.eli5: Kids can add a wish to the list, like a game with no running. The other side may pick a game that fits the wish, and then they double-check the list.

sections.title: What the Protection Guarantees
sections.content:
The list can only be protected if the selected mechanism provides integrity. If it does not, an active attacker can force use of a mechanism that is acceptable to the target but not mutually preferred.

When per-message integrity is available and an adversary altered the list so a not-mutually-preferred mechanism could be chosen, the protocol guarantees two things. If the initiator sends the last mechanism token, both peers fail. If the acceptor sends it, the acceptor does not complete and the initiator, at worst, completes with its own preferred mechanism. If the alteration had no material impact, negotiation may continue.

SPNEGO is no stronger than the integrity protection of the weakest mechanism acceptable to the peers. It does not generally defeat downgrade attacks between mechanisms whose tokens look alike and depend on an unprotected OID. Peers also remain exposed to denial of service.
sections.eli5: The check works only if the game has a way to spot cheating. A cheater can still stop the game, but they cannot quietly make you play a worse one.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2478
sections.content:
The appendix on changes records why this document differs from RFC 2478. Microsoft Windows 2000, Windows XP and Windows Server 2003 implementations produce no mechlistMIC and ignore any they receive, and may use an incorrect Kerberos V5 OID (1.2.840.48018.1.2.2). To work with them, NegTokenTarg became negTokenResp for all later messages, NegTokenInit is only the first message, mechTypes is no longer optional, and the MIC may be omitted when the selected mechanism is the first choice of both peers.

To fix RFC 2478 itself, reqFlags is treated as unprotected, DER is required, the GSS_GetMIC() input is clarified, per-message integrity is requested for the negotiated mechanism, and one MIC is exchanged in each direction.

The authors state the cost: a conforming implementation will not interoperate with a strict RFC 2478 implementation. They chose security between new implementations and compatibility with deployed ones, noting that the working group knew of no deployed RFC 2478 implementations on the Internet.
sections.eli5: The rules were fixed to match how the popular programs really behaved. The price is that the new rules no longer match the very oldest written version.

viz.caption: SPNEGO EXCHANGE, SIMPLIFIED FROM RFC 4178 SECTIONS 3 AND 5

messages.label: negTokenInit
messages.note: mechTypes in preference order, plus the optimistic mechToken.

messages.label: negTokenResp
messages.note: negState and supportedMech, plus any response token.

messages.label: mechanism tokens
messages.note: The selected mechanism's tokens continue inside negotiation messages.

messages.label: mechListMIC
messages.note: Exchanged when required; optional if the mechanism is both peers' first choice.

items.label: accept-completed
items.desc: No further message expected from the peer; context established for the sender.

items.label: accept-incomplete
items.desc: At least one more message from the peer is needed.

items.label: request-mic
items.desc: MIC exchange will be required; only in the first reply from the target.

data.title: NegTokenInit
data.code:
NegTokenInit ::= SEQUENCE {
    mechTypes       [0] MechTypeList,
    reqFlags        [1] ContextFlags  OPTIONAL,
      -- inherited from RFC 2478 for backward compatibility,
      -- RECOMMENDED to be left out
    mechToken       [2] OCTET STRING  OPTIONAL,
    mechListMIC     [3] OCTET STRING  OPTIONAL,
    ...
}
